lesson.title: Cell replacement therapy
lesson.scope: Relate stem cell differentiation to replacement of damaged or lost cells.
lesson.subtitle: 27 pages · original diagrams · written practice

screens.title: The Biological Repair Kit
screens.html:
The Biological Repair Kit

What if, instead of just managing symptoms with drugs, we could simply replace the damaged cells in a person's body?

Imagine 'patching' a heart after an attack or regrowing neurons lost to Alzheimer's disease.

screens.title: DEFINITION
screens.html:
DEFINITION

🧠

What is Cell Replacement Therapy?

Cell Replacement Therapy (CRT) involves the transplantation of healthy cells into a patient to replace or repair tissue that is damaged or diseased.

Remember

The goal is to restore normal function to the organ or tissue using the body's own biological building blocks: stem cells.

screens.title: Regenerative Medicine Goals
screens.html:
Regenerative Medicine Goals

CRT is a pillar of Regenerative Medicine, aiming for ambitious outcomes:

Restoration: Restoring function to damaged organs.

Integration: Ensuring cells function seamlessly with host tissue.

Long-term Cure: Moving from symptom management to permanent repair.

screens.title: The Power of Stem Cells
screens.html:
The Power of Stem Cells

Stem cells are the 'unspecialized' precursors that make CRT possible. They possess two unique characteristics:

Self-renewal: The ability to divide and create more stem cells.

Potency: The ability to differentiate into specialized cell types.

screens.title: CELL SOURCES
screens.html:
CELL SOURCES

⚠️

Embryonic Stem Cells (ESCs)

Sourced from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst (an embryo roughly 5 days old). They are pluripotent, meaning they can become almost any cell type in the human body.

Watch out

Because they are pluripotent, ESCs are highly versatile but carry a risk of forming tumours (teratomas) if growth is not controlled.

screens.title: Adult Stem Cells (ASCs)
screens.html:
🔍

Adult Stem Cells (ASCs)

Found in small numbers in various adult tissues like bone marrow, skin, and the brain. They are multipotent, meaning they can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types related to their tissue of origin.

Example

Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow can become red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets, but they cannot become nerve cells.

screens.title: Comparing Stem Cell Sources
screens.html:
Comparing Stem Cell Sources

Embryonic (ESCs)

Potency: Pluripotent

Growth: Easily grown in culture

Rejection: High risk (foreign DNA)

Adult (ASCs)

Potency: Multipotent

Growth: Difficult to isolate

Rejection: Low risk (can use patient’s own cells)

screens.title: The iPSC Revolution
screens.html:
🔑

The iPSC Revolution

In 2006, scientists discovered they could 'reprogramme' adult skin cells back into a state identical to embryonic stem cells. These are called Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs).

Key point

This avoids the ethical issues of using embryos while allowing for 'patient-specific' cells that won't be rejected by the immune system.

screens.title: Creating iPSCs
screens.html:
Creating iPSCs

Viral vectors insert specific 'reprogramming genes' into adult somatic cells.

Harvesting Skin or blood cells are collected from the patient.

Reprogramming Genes are introduced to reset the cell's DNA identity.

Expansion The resulting iPSCs are cultured into billions of copies.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

🔍

Directing Differentiation

Once we have stem cells, we must 'tell' them what to become. This is done by adding specific growth factors and chemical signals to the culture medium.

Example

Adding 'Neural Growth Factor' encourages stem cells to differentiate into neurons for treating conditions like Parkinson's.

screens.title: Treating Parkinson's Disease
screens.html:
🔑

Treating Parkinson's Disease

Parkinson's is caused by the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain.

In CRT, stem cells are differentiated into these specific neurons and surgically implanted into the patient's midbrain.

Key point

The goal is for new cells to establish connections and take over the production of dopamine.

screens.title: Diabetes & Islet Cells
screens.html:
Diabetes & Islet Cells

In Type 1 Diabetes, the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas.

CRT aims to create and transplant new beta cells, potentially curing the patient by allowing them to regulate their own blood glucose again.

screens.title: The Ethical Debate
screens.html:
The Ethical Debate

The use of Embryonic Stem Cells remains one of the most debated topics in science due to questions regarding the moral status of the embryo.

screens.title: Points of Contention
screens.html:
Points of Contention

Arguments For

Potential to cure previously incurable diseases.

Use of 'spare' embryos from IVF that would otherwise be destroyed.

Relief of human suffering.

Arguments Against

View that life begins at conception.

The embryo is destroyed during extraction.

Fear of a 'slippery slope' toward commodification of embryos.

screens.title: Ethical Evolution
screens.html:
Ethical Evolution

Has the discovery of iPSCs solved the ethical dilemma?

While iPSCs avoid using embryos, they raise new questions about genetic privacy and the potential to create reproductive cells (gametes) from skin.

screens.title: CURRENT BARRIERS
screens.html:
CURRENT BARRIERS

Technical Challenges

CRT is not yet standard. Key hurdles include:

Controlling differentiation to prevent errors.

Avoiding immune rejection via patient cells.

Integrating with nerve or blood networks.

screens.title: Future Horizons
screens.html:
Future Horizons

Research is moving toward 3D Bioprinting, where stem cells are printed layer by layer onto a 'scaffold' to grow entire replacement organs, like bladders or heart valves.

screens.title: Evaluative Reflection
screens.html:
Evaluative Reflection

If iPSCs provide a way to create versatile stem cells without embryos, should embryonic stem cell research be banned? Justify your position considering scientific progress versus moral concerns.

screens.title: Evaluative Reflection
screens.html:
Evaluative Reflection

You might have said...

iPSCs are not yet perfect; ESCs remain the gold standard for pluripotency.

Banning research may delay breakthroughs for Parkinson's or Alzheimer's.

If iPSCs match ESC results, destroying embryos may lose moral justification.

Compare viral vector risks in iPSCs against rejection risks in ESCs.

screens.title: Lesson Summary
screens.html:
Lesson Summary

What we covered:

CRT aims to replace damaged cells to restore function.

ESCs are pluripotent but raise significant ethical concerns.

ASCs are multipotent and restricted in use.

iPSCs offer a way to create pluripotent cells from the patient's own tissue.

Current targets include Parkinson's and Type 1 Diabetes.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain two requirements for replacement cells to restore tissue function and identify one risk.
steps: Replacement cells must differentiate into an appropriate cell type and perform the needed specialised function.
Cells must survive, integrate and receive suitable support in the recipient tissue.
Immune rejection, uncontrolled growth or inappropriate differentiation may reduce safety or effectiveness.

bank.q: What is cell replacement therapy intended to do?
o: Restore function using suitable replacement cells
bank.why: The aim is to replace or restore cells whose loss or damage reduces tissue function.

o: Copying DNA without change in cell type
bank.why: Differentiation produces specialised structures and functions through changes in gene expression.

bank.q: Which is a possible risk of cell transplantation?
bank.why: Transplanted cells may trigger immune rejection; inappropriate growth and other complications also require evaluation.
